title: Apps and Software with JavaScript
blurb: Build real tools for work and data: to-do lists, tables, charts, sound and timers, and how desktop and phone apps are designed.
intro:
Most software isn't games. It's tools: to-do lists, spreadsheets, budget trackers, music players, timers. This module shows how those apps are designed and how to build them with JavaScript.

You'll learn the kinds of apps, how desktop, phone and web apps differ, and the parts of an app window. Then you'll do the one thing every app does: keep the data in an array and render it to the screen. You'll add, edit, delete, search, sort, total up, import and export data, build Undo, draw bar, line and pie charts, play notes with the Web Audio API and make a stopwatch. The boss stage is a complete pocket money tracker.

Keep it simple

Every app here is the same loop: something happens → change the data → render. Once that clicks, you can build almost any tool. Try your own in the .

stages.hook: Games are for fun. But most of the code in the world runs tools: calendars, calculators, music players, spreadsheets, chat apps. People use them to get something done. In this module you'll design and build tools like these with JavaScript.
stages.l:
The words get mixed up a lot, so here's how people usually use them:

WordWhat it meansExample
SoftwareAny program that runs on a computer or phoneEverything below, plus things like Windows itself
App (application)Software you use to do a task: write, plan, calculate, listenNotes, Calculator, Spotify, Google Sheets
WebsitePages you mostly read and click throughA news site, a school's home page
Web appAn app that runs in a browser tabGoogle Docs, Canva, Figma

The difference between a website and a web app is mostly about what you do there. On a website you read. In an app you make and change things, and the app remembers them.
stages.p: Four things a student uses on a school laptop.
stages.q: Which one is an app rather than a website?
opts: A page that lists the school's opening hours
A budget tracker where you add what you spend and it totals it up
A news article about a football match
miss: You only read the opening hours. Nothing you do changes or gets saved.
You read an article, you don't make anything with it.
An About page is for reading.
stages.why: In the budget tracker you put data in, the app works something out (the total), and it remembers it for next time. Input, processing and saving are what make something an app.
stages.h: Where do you make or change something that the program keeps?

stages.l:
Apps that aren't games mostly fall into a few families. Each family has its own habits:

FamilyExamplesWhat it's built around
ProductivityTo-do lists, notes, calendarsA list of items you add, edit, tick off and delete
DataSpreadsheets, dashboards, budget trackers, fitness logsTables of numbers, totals and charts
MediaMusic players, audio editors, photo editorsSound or pictures, with controls like play, volume and filters
CommunicationChat, email, video callsMessages arriving and being sent
UtilitiesCalculator, timer, unit converter, password generatorOne small job, done fast
Tip

Before you design an app, write one sentence: This app helps [who] to [do what]. If you can't fill it in, you're not ready to draw buttons yet.
stages.p: A student wants to build an app where runners type in each run's distance and time, then see a chart of how they're improving.
miss: Nobody is sending messages to anyone.
There's no sound or pictures to edit.
It does more than one quick job: it keeps a history and charts it.
stages.why: It stores rows of numbers (runs), works things out from them (pace, totals) and shows a chart. That's a data app, like a tiny spreadsheet built for one purpose.
stages.h: Look at what the app is built around: lists, numbers, sound, messages, or one quick job?

stages.l:
JavaScript started in the browser, but now it runs nearly everywhere. The same skills build all three kinds of app:

KindRuns onHow JavaScript gets thereReal examples
Web appAny browserPlain HTML, CSS and JavaScriptGoogle Docs, Canva
Desktop appWindows, Mac, LinuxElectron wraps a web app in its own window with a built-in browserVS Code, Discord, Slack, Figma's desktop app
Mobile appPhones and tabletsReact Native or Capacitor turn JavaScript into a phone appParts of Instagram, Discord's phone app
Installable web app (PWA)Browser, but with its own icon and offline modeA web app plus a small file describing its name and iconTwitter/X Lite, Starbucks ordering

So the to-do list you'll build in this module could, with one of these tools, become a real desktop or phone app.
stages.p: A team has a working web app. They want people to download it and open it from their Windows and Mac taskbar, in its own window.
stages.q: What would most JavaScript teams use?
opts: Rewrite it in a different language for each system
miss: That works, but it's two whole new apps to write and fix.
A website still lives in a browser tab, not its own window.
A PDF can't run code.
stages.why: Electron bundles the web app with its own browser engine, so the same HTML, CSS and JavaScript become a desktop app. VS Code, the editor many programmers use every day, is built this way.
stages.h: Look at the Desktop row of the table.

stages.l:
Just like web pages, app windows have parts with names. Most desktop apps (and big web apps like Gmail) use the same layout:

PartWhat it holds
Toolbar (or app bar)The app's name and the most-used actions: New, Search, Share
SidebarNavigation: folders, playlists, channels, pages
Main area (or content pane)The thing you're working on right now
Status barSmall facts about what's happening: how many items, whether it's saved
Dialog (or modal)A box that pops up and asks a question before you continue
ToastA short message that slides in and disappears by itself: Note deleted · Undo

This layout is called list and detail: pick something from the list on the left, see it on the right. Email, music players, file managers and chat apps all use it.
stages.p: Look at the Notes app.
stages.html:
A📝 Notes
B
All notes
Shopping
Homework
Ideas
C
Homework

Maths p.42, read chapter 3…

D3 notes · Saved ✓
miss: A is the toolbar, with the app name and main actions.
B is the sidebar, the list of notes.
C is the main area, showing the note you picked.
stages.why: D is the status bar. It quietly tells you things like 3 notes · Saved ✓ so you never wonder whether your work is safe.
stages.h: Status bars usually sit along the very bottom and show small facts.

stages.l:
On a phone, you design for a thumb, not a mouse. A few rules every mobile designer follows:

  • Big tap targets. Apple says buttons should be at least 44 by 44 points, and Google says 48 by 48. Smaller than that and people tap the wrong thing.
  • The thumb zone. Holding a phone in one hand, your thumb easily reaches the bottom middle of the screen. The top corners are a stretch. That's why phone apps put the main navigation in a bottom tab bar.
  • One column. Sidebars don't fit. The list and the detail become two separate screens.
Tip

Hold your phone in one hand and try to tap the top-left corner with your thumb. Now you know why the Back button is the one everyone hates.
stages.p: Here's a phone budget app. People say adding a new expense is fiddly.
stages.html:
Budget
Spent this week
$42.50
Food $20 · Bus $12 · Games $10.50
A
B🏠📊⚙️
opts: A: the tiny + button in the top corner
B: the tab bar along the bottom
The big total in the middle
miss: The bottom tab bar is right where thumbs rest. That's a good choice.
The total is easy to read. You don't need to tap it.
The header color is fine and has good contrast.
stages.why: The + is the app's most important action, but it's tiny and in the hardest place to reach. A big round + button near the bottom (Google calls it a floating action button) would fix both problems.
stages.h: Think about size (44 to 48 points) and where a thumb can reach easily.

stages.l:
Here's the most important idea in app building. An app has two parts:

  • The data (also called state): plain JavaScript values, usually an array of objects, that say what's true right now.
  • The view: what's drawn on the screen.
// the data: the single source of truth
let tasks = [
  { id: 1, text: "Feed the cat", done: true },
  { id: 2, text: "Maths homework", done: false }
];

Every app follows the same loop: something happens (a click, a key), the code changes the data, then a render() function redraws the screen from the data. You never change the screen by itself and hope the data keeps up.

Big tools like React and Vue are built around exactly this loop. They just do the redrawing for you.
stages.p: A student's to-do app has no tasks array. To count unfinished tasks, it reads the words off the screen and checks which ones have a line through them.
stages.q: Why is keeping the data in an array better?
opts: Arrays make the app look nicer
The array is the single source of truth, so saving, counting and searching all work from the same plain values
It makes the app slower but safer
miss: The data doesn't change how anything looks.
Screens show text fine. The problem is using them as storage.
It actually makes the app faster and simpler.
stages.why: With an array you can save it, count it, sort it and search it in one line each. Reading things back off the screen breaks as soon as you change the design. Data first, screen second.
stages.h: What happens to the counting code if someone changes how finished tasks look?

stages.l:
Almost every app does four things to its data. Programmers call them CRUD:

LetterActionIn a contacts app
CreateAdd a new itemAdd a friend's number
ReadShow or find itemsScroll the list, search for a name
UpdateChange an itemFix a typo in a name
DeleteRemove an itemRemove an old contact

Once you can do CRUD on an array of objects, you can build to-do lists, address books, shopping lists, gradebooks and inventories. They're all the same app wearing different clothes.
stages.p: In a music app, you rename a playlist from Chill to Homework Beats.
miss: No new playlist was made. The same one got a new name.
You changed something, not just looked at it.
The playlist is still there.
stages.why: Changing something that already exists is an update. In code, that's finding the playlist by its id and changing its name.
stages.h: Was something added, looked at, changed or removed?

stages.l:
In 1994 Jakob Nielsen wrote 10 rules of thumb for usable software. They're still used today. Four of them matter in every app you'll build:

RuleWhat it means
Show what's happeningSaving… Saved ✓. Loading spinners. A count of items. Never leave people guessing.
Let people undoEveryone clicks the wrong thing. Give them an easy way back.
Prevent mistakesGrey out a Save button until the form is filled in. Ask before deleting something big.
Speak humanCouldn't save, you're offline, not Error 0x80004005.

One more habit: design the empty state. A brand new to-do list shouldn't be a blank white box. Say Nothing here yet. Add your first task above!
stages.p: In a notes app, it's easy to delete a note by accident, and people get upset when they lose one.
opts: Show a pop-up on every delete asking "Are you SURE?"
Delete it, then show a toast: "Note deleted · Undo" for a few seconds
Make the delete button tiny so it's hard to hit
miss: Then people can never tidy up.
People get so used to clicking Yes that they stop reading. It also slows down every delete.
Tiny buttons make mistakes more likely, not less.
stages.why: An undo toast keeps deleting fast for people who meant it, and gives a way back to people who didn't. Gmail, Google Docs and most phone apps do this. Save the "Are you sure?" box for things that really can't be undone.
stages.h: Which option keeps deleting quick and lets people take it back?

stages.hook: Now the code. Every app in this module stores its data the same way: an array of objects, one object per item. Each object is called a record, and each one gets an id so you can find it again later.
stages.l:
const songs = [
  { id: 1, title: "Sunrise", plays: 12, liked: true },
  { id: 2, title: "Night Bus", plays: 3, liked: false }
];
const liked = songs.filter(s => s.liked);
console.log(liked.length + " liked songs");
1 liked songs

filter keeps the records that pass a test. .length counts them.
stages.p: Write countLeft(tasks). Each task looks like { id, text, done }. Return how many tasks are not done yet. This is the 2 left you see at the bottom of a to-do app.
stages.h: Filter for tasks where done is false (!t.done), then return the length.

stages.l:
To create a record, build a new object and push it onto the array. Good apps also prevent mistakes: nobody wants a blank task that's only spaces.

function addSong(songs, title, id) {
  const clean = title.trim();
  if (clean === "") return songs;   // nothing to add
  songs.push({ id: id, title: clean, plays: 0, liked: false });
  return songs;
}

.trim() cuts spaces off both ends, so " hi " becomes "hi" and " " becomes "".
stages.p: Write addTask(tasks, text, id). Trim the text. If it's empty, return tasks unchanged. Otherwise push { id: id, text: (the trimmed text), done: false } onto the end and return tasks.
stages.h: Same shape as addSong, but the new object has id, text and done: false.

stages.l:
To update a record, find it by its id and change it. find returns the first record that passes a test, or undefined if none do.

function likeSong(songs, id) {
  const song = songs.find(s => s.id === id);
  if (song) song.liked = true;
  return songs;
}

Why ids and not positions? Positions change when you sort, filter or delete. An id stays with its record forever.
stages.p: Write toggle(tasks, id). Find the task with that id and flip its done (true becomes false, false becomes true). If no task has that id, change nothing. Return tasks.
stages.h: Find it like likeSong does. To flip a boolean, set it to ! itself: task.done = !task.done.

stages.l: Deleting usually means building a new array without the record. filter is perfect for that: keep everything whose id is not the one you're deleting.
stages.p: What does this print?
miss: That's the one being removed. filter keeps the ones that pass the test, and Shopping fails it.
The note with id 7 fails the test, so it's left out.
Homework's id is 9, which isn't 7, so it stays.
stages.why: n.id !== 7 is true for Ideas and Homework, so they stay. Shopping is the only one that fails the test. Then map pulls out the titles and join puts commas between them.
stages.h: Go through each note: is its id not equal to 7? Keep the ones where the answer is yes.

stages.p: Write removeTask(tasks, id). Return a new array with every task except the one with that id.
stages.h: One line with filter. Keep tasks whose id is not equal to id.
stages.st:
function removeTask(tasks, id) {
}

stages.l:
A search box is a filter that runs every time you type. Good search ignores capital letters and stray spaces, so ava, AVA and Ava all find Ava.

const word = "  NIGHT ".trim().toLowerCase();   // "night"
console.log("Night Bus".toLowerCase().includes(word));
true

An empty search should show everything. Luckily, every string includes the empty string "", so that happens on its own.
stages.p: Write search(people, query). Each person is { name, phone }. Return the people whose name contains the query, ignoring capitals and spaces around the query.
stages.h: Clean the query once (trim then toLowerCase), then filter people where p.name.toLowerCase().includes(q).

stages.l:
Click a column heading in a spreadsheet or file manager and the rows sort by that column. Click again and it flips. sort takes a compare function that gets two rows and returns a negative number if a goes first, a positive number if b goes first, or 0 if they're tied.

const byPlays = songs.slice().sort((a, b) => {
  if (a.plays < b.plays) return -1;
  if (a.plays > b.plays) return 1;
  return 0;
});

slice() makes a copy first, because sort changes the array it's called on. Using < and > works for numbers and for text.
stages.p: Write sortBy(rows, key, dir). Return a sorted copy of rows, sorted by the property named key. If dir is "asc", smallest first. If it's "desc", biggest first.
stages.h: Read the values with a[key] and b[key]. Work out the result like the example, then if dir is "desc", return the opposite (multiply by -1).

stages.l:
Data apps are always adding things up: total spent, total minutes, total steps. reduce walks through an array carrying a running total.

const minutes = [{ min: 20 }, { min: 35 }, { min: 15 }];
const all = minutes.reduce((sum, m) => sum + m.min, 0);
console.log(all);
70

The 0 at the end is where the total starts.

Watch out

Computers store decimals slightly wrong: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004! Money apps round to cents at the end: Math.round(x * 100) / 100.
stages.p: Write total(items). Each item has an amount. Return the sum of all the amounts, rounded to cents (2 decimal places) as a number.
stages.h: Use reduce like the minutes example, then round the result with Math.round(sum * 100) / 100.
stages.st:
function total(items) {
}

stages.l:
"How much did I spend on food?" To answer that, apps group records by a property into an object, one key per group.

const counts = {};
for (const song of songs) {
  const g = song.genre;
  counts[g] = (counts[g] || 0) + 1;   // start at 0 the first time
}
// { pop: 3, rock: 1 }

counts[g] || 0 means "what's there already, or 0 if this is the first one".
stages.p: Write byCategory(items). Each item has cat and amount. Return an object with one key per category, holding the total amount for that category.
stages.h: Same loop as the genre example, but add item.amount instead of 1, and use item.cat as the key.

stages.l:
People read $1,234.50 instantly. 1234.5 makes them squint. JavaScript has a built-in number formatter, Intl.NumberFormat, that knows how every country writes numbers and money:

const euros = new Intl.NumberFormat("de-DE", { style: "currency", currency: "EUR" });
console.log(euros.format(1234.5));
1.234,50 €

Germany uses a dot for thousands and a comma for cents! The formatter handles that for you. For the US, use "en-US" and "USD".

Tip

For a quick fixed number of decimals without commas, n.toFixed(2) turns 3.5 into the string "3.50".
stages.p: Write money(n) that returns n as US dollars, like $1,234.50.
stages.h: Make a formatter like the euro one, with "en-US" and currency: "USD", and return .format(n).
stages.st:
function money(n) {
}

stages.l:
Timers, music players and video editors all show time as minutes:seconds. Two tools help:

console.log(Math.floor(130 / 60));   // whole minutes in 130 seconds
console.log(130 % 60);               // seconds left over
console.log(String(7).padStart(3, "0"));
2
10
007

% gives the remainder after dividing. padStart(length, "0") adds zeros to the front until the string is long enough.
stages.p: Write mmss(seconds) that turns a whole number of seconds into a string like 02:05. Both parts always have 2 digits.
stages.h: Minutes are Math.floor(seconds / 60), seconds are seconds % 60. Turn each into a string, pad to length 2, and join with ":".
stages.st:
function mmss(seconds) {
}

stages.l:
Spreadsheets, banks and fitness watches can all export data as CSV (comma-separated values). It's just text: the first line names the columns, and each line after that is one row.

date,steps
Mon,8200
Tue,10450

Reading it is a job for split:

const lines = "a,b\n1,2".split("\n");   // ["a,b", "1,2"]
const cells = lines[1].split(",");       // ["1", "2"]

Every cell comes out as a string. Turn number columns into numbers with Number(...) when you need to do maths.
stages.p: Write parseCSV(text). Return an array with one object per row (not counting the header). Use the header names as the keys. Leave the values as strings. Ignore empty lines.
stages.h: Split into lines and drop empty ones. The first line split by commas gives the keys. For each other line, split it and build an object where row[keys[i]] = cells[i].

stages.l:
Going the other way lets people open your app's data in Excel or Google Sheets. Object.keys gives you the column names, and join glues things together.

const pet = { name: "Rex", age: 4 };
console.log(Object.keys(pet).join(" | "));
console.log(Object.keys(pet).map(k => pet[k]).join(" | "));
name | age
Rex | 4
stages.p: Write toCSV(rows). The first line is the keys of the first row, joined with commas. Then one line per row with its values in the same order. Join the lines with "\n". If there are no rows, return "".
stages.h: Get keys from rows[0]. Build an array starting with keys.join(","), add keys.map(k => row[k]).join(",") for each row, then join that array with "\n".
stages.st:
function toCSV(rows) {
}

stages.l:
Apps remember things between visits with localStorage, which only stores text. If you hand it an array of objects, it turns it into text the lazy way, and your data is gone. The fix is JSON.stringify to save and JSON.parse to load.

localStorage.setItem("songs", JSON.stringify(songs));        // save
const back = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("songs") || "[]");  // load
stages.p: This fake store works just like localStorage: it turns whatever you give it into a string. What does this print?
opts:
Feed the cat
Feed the cat
miss: Without JSON.stringify, String() doesn't know how to write an object out.
Neither line pulls out just the text.
Something is stored for a. It's just not useful.
stages.why: String() on an object gives the useless [object Object], and the task is lost. JSON.stringify writes out the whole structure, so JSON.parse can rebuild it later.
stages.h: Try String({ a: 1 }) in your head. It's not what you'd hope.

stages.l:
How does Undo work? Before every change, the app saves a copy of the data onto a history array (a stack). Undo pops the last copy off and puts it back.

function rename(app, name) {
  app.history.push(app.title);   // remember the old value first
  app.title = name;
  return app;
}

pop() removes the last thing from an array and gives it back to you. Last in, first out, just like a stack of plates.
stages.p: Write undo(app). app has items (the current list) and history (an array of older lists). If history is empty, return app unchanged. Otherwise pop the last list off history, make it the new items, and return app.
stages.h: Check app.history.length === 0 first. Then app.items = app.history.pop();

stages.l: For Undo to work, every change has to save a copy of the list before it changes anything. slice() makes the copy. Without it, history would hold the very same array that keeps changing.
stages.p: Tap the lines into order so addWithHistory(app, text) saves a copy of app.items onto app.history, then adds text to the items.
stages.h: Save first, change second. If you push the text first, the saved copy already has the new item in it, and Undo does nothing.

stages.t: Draw the list from the data
stages.hook: Time to put it on screen. Remember the loop: change the data, then render. The render function is the bridge between your array and what people see.
stages.l:
A render function does the same three things every time: clear the old view, build a piece of screen for each record, and update any totals.

const names = ["Ava", "Ben"];
const ul = document.querySelector("#people");
function show() {
  ul.innerHTML = "";                         // 1. clear
  for (const n of names) {                   // 2. build one li per name
    const item = document.createElement("li");
    item.textContent = n;
    ul.append(item);
  }
}
show();
Why clear first?

Render runs again after every change. Without clearing, each run would add the whole list again underneath the old one.
stages.p: Finish render(). For each task, make an li with a span inside holding the task's text. Give the li the class done if the task is done, and set li.dataset.id to the task's id (you'll need it later). Then put 2 left (the number of unfinished tasks) in #count.
stages.h: Clear list.innerHTML, loop over tasks, build li and span with document.createElement, use classList.add("done") when t.done, and append the span to the li and the li to the list. For the count, filter for !t.done and add " left".
stages.html: ✅ My Tasks

stages.l:
The create part of CRUD usually comes from a form. Listening for submit on the form (not click on the button) means pressing Enter works too.

noteForm.addEventListener("submit", e => {
  e.preventDefault();               // don't reload the page
  const title = noteBox.value.trim();
  if (title === "") return;         // prevent empty notes
  notes.push({ id: nextNote++, title: title });
  drawNotes();
  noteBox.value = "";               // ready for the next one
});

nextNote++ uses the current number, then adds 1, so every record gets a new id.
stages.p: When #add is submitted, add a task with the trimmed text from #text, the next id and done: false, then render and clear the box. Ignore empty or spaces-only text.
stages.h: Same shape as the notes example, using form, box, tasks, nextId and render from the starter.
stages.html: ✅ My Tasks

stages.l:
You could add a click listener to every li, but render throws them away and makes new ones each time. Instead, put one listener on the list and ask which item was clicked. This is called event delegation.

palette.addEventListener("click", e => {
  const swatch = e.target.closest("[data-color]");   // the swatch that was clicked, or null
  if (!swatch) return;                               // clicked a gap
  paint(swatch.dataset.color);
});

closest() walks up from what was clicked (maybe the span) to the nearest match. dataset values are always strings, so use Number() to compare with number ids.
stages.p: Clicking a task should flip its done and render again. Use one click listener on #list.
stages.h: In the listener: const li = e.target.closest("li"), stop if it's null, then find the task whose id is Number(li.dataset.id), flip done, and call render().
stages.html: ✅ My Tasks

stages.l:
The input event fires every time the text in a box changes, so the list can filter as you type. That instant feedback is what makes search feel fast.

colorBox.addEventListener("input", () => {
  swatch.style.background = colorBox.value;
});

Don't forget the empty state: when nothing matches, say so.
stages.p: Every time #q changes, render only the people whose name contains what's typed, ignoring capitals and spaces around it. render already shows No matches when the list is empty.
stages.h: Add an input listener on q. Inside, clean q.value with trim and toLowerCase, filter people like you did in the Search box logic stage, and pass the result to render.
stages.html:
📇 Contacts

    No matches.

stages.l:
Tables are the heart of data apps. People expect to click a column heading to sort, and click it again to flip the order. The app has to remember which column is sorted and which way: that's more state.

let view = "grid";
viewBtn.addEventListener("click", () => {
  view = view === "grid" ? "list" : "grid";   // flip between two values
  drawFiles();
});
stages.p: Clicking a heading (th with data-key) sorts rows by that key. If it's the same key as last time, flip sortDir. If it's a new key, start with "asc". Then render.
stages.h: Listen for clicks on #head and use e.target.closest("th"). Read th.dataset.key. Update sortDir and sortKey, then rows.sort(...) with a compare function that checks sortDir, and call render().
stages.html:
📊 Scores
Name ⇅Score ⇅

stages.l: A student's shopping list app works the first time. But every time they add an item, the whole list appears again underneath.
stages.p: Fix the bug so adding an item shows each item exactly once.
stages.h: Look at what render does before its loop. Remember the three steps of a render function.
stages.html: 🛒 Shopping

stages.l:
Remember the friendliest delete? Remove it right away, then show a toast with an Undo button. To undo, the app needs to remember what it removed and where it was.

const pos = songs.findIndex(s => s.id === id);   // where it is
lastRemoved = { song: songs[pos], pos: pos };       // remember it
songs.splice(pos, 1);                               // take 1 item out at pos
// later, to put it back:
songs.splice(lastRemoved.pos, 0, lastRemoved.song); // insert at pos, removing 0

splice(start, howMany, ...newItems) can remove and insert items anywhere in an array.
stages.p: Clicking a task's ✕ (class del) removes it, renders, and shows #toast with Deleted: (the task's text) in #toastMsg. Clicking #undo puts the task back in the same place, renders, and hides the toast.
stages.h: In a click listener on list: check e.target.matches(".del"), find the task's position with findIndex using the li's dataset.id, save it in lastRemoved, splice it out, render, and show the toast. In the undo listener, splice it back in.
stages.html: ✅ My Tasks

stages.l:
People who use an app all day love keyboard shortcuts. Many apps (YouTube, GitHub, Gmail) jump to the search box when you press /, and Esc gets you out again.

document.addEventListener("keydown", e => {
  if (e.key === "?") {
    helpBox.hidden = false;
    e.preventDefault();       // stop the key doing its normal job
  }
});

e.key is the key that was pressed, like "a", "/", "Enter" or "Escape". Real apps also skip shortcuts while you're typing in a box, so / still types a slash there.
stages.p: Pressing / should focus #q (and preventDefault, so no slash gets typed). Pressing Escape should clear #q and take the focus away from it with blur().
stages.h: One keydown listener on document. If e.key === "/", call q.focus() and e.preventDefault(). If it's "Escape", set q.value = "" and call q.blur().

📇 ContactsPress / to search
  • Ava Patel
  • Ben Okafor
stages.st: const q = document.querySelector("#q");

stages.hook: A table of 365 numbers is hard to read. A chart of the same numbers can be understood in one second. That's why every data app has charts.
stages.l:
Each chart type answers a different question:

ChartAnswersExample
Bar chartWhich is bigger? (comparing groups)Spending per category
Line chartHow did it change over time?Steps per day this month
Pie or donutWhat share of the whole is each part? (2 to 5 parts only)How your day is split up
Scatter plotAre two things related?Hours of sleep vs test score

Two rules that keep charts honest: bars start at zero (otherwise small differences look huge), and label everything: a title, the units, and what each color means.
stages.p: A fitness app wants to show how your resting heart rate changed every week for a year.
miss: A pie shows parts of a whole. 52 slices would be unreadable.
Tables are good for exact lookups, not for spotting a trend.
Scatter plots compare two different measurements.
stages.why: "How did it change over time?" is exactly what line charts are for. The eye follows the line and sees the trend straight away.
stages.h: Look at the Answers column. What question is the app trying to answer?

stages.l:
Every chart has to turn data values into pixel sizes. The trick is a ratio: how big is this value compared to the biggest one?

// a progress ring: 30 of 120 minutes done, ring is 360 degrees
const degrees = 30 / 120 * 360;
console.log(degrees);
90

The same idea makes the biggest bar fill the whole chart and every other bar the right size next to it.
stages.p: Write barHeight(value, max, height) that returns how many pixels tall a bar should be, rounded to a whole number. The biggest value (max) gets the full height. If max is 0, return 0 (so you never divide by zero).
stages.h: value / max is the fraction. Multiply by height and round with Math.round. Check for max === 0 first.
stages.st:
function barHeight(value, max, height) {
}

stages.t: A bar chart on a canvas
stages.l:
For charts with lots of data, apps draw on a <canvas>. Here canvas and ctx are ready for you. Remember: y goes down, so a bar standing on a baseline at y 140 starts at 140 - h.

// one bar, 80 pixels tall, standing on y = 140
ctx.fillStyle = "#e85d75";
ctx.fillRect(20, 140 - 80, 30, 80);   // x, y, width, height

Loops make charts: one rectangle per data value, each one shifted along x.
stages.p: Draw one bar per value in data, colored #2f6fec. Bar i starts at x 20 + i * 60 and is 40 wide. Use barHeight(value, max, 120) for its height, and stand every bar on y 140.
stages.h: Loop with data.forEach((v, i) => { ... }). Work out h with barHeight, then ctx.fillRect(20 + i * 60, 140 - h, 40, h). Set the color once before the loop.

stages.l:
A line chart is points joined up. Canvas draws lines with a path: start with beginPath(), moveTo the first point, lineTo each next point, then stroke() to draw it.

ctx.beginPath();
ctx.moveTo(10, 100);     // pick up the pen here
ctx.lineTo(60, 40);      // draw to here
ctx.lineTo(110, 70);     // and on to here
ctx.strokeStyle = "green";
ctx.lineWidth = 2;
ctx.stroke();

Dots on each point make the values easy to spot. Draw a circle with ctx.arc(x, y, radius, 0, Math.PI * 2) and fill().
stages.p: Point i is at x 20 + i * 45 and y 140 - barHeight(steps[i], max, 120). Draw a line through all the points (#2f6fec, width 3), then a dot on each point (#f28c28, radius 5).
stages.h: Make a helper that returns { x, y } for index i. Path: beginPath, moveTo point 0, lineTo the rest, set the style, stroke. Then a loop where each dot gets its own beginPath, arc and fill.

stages.l:
A pie chart shows each part as a share of the whole. First add everything up, then each slice is its value divided by the total. Times 100 gives a percent, and times 360 gives the slice's angle in degrees.

const day = { sleep: 9, school: 7, other: 8 };   // 24 hours
console.log(day.school / 24 * 100);
29.166666666666668
Drawing it

On a canvas, each slice is ctx.moveTo(cx, cy) then ctx.arc(cx, cy, r, start, end), where angles are in radians: a full circle is Math.PI * 2. Each slice starts where the last one ended.
stages.p: Write shares(values). Return a new array with each value as a whole-number percent of the total (use Math.round). If the total is 0, return all zeros.
stages.h: Get the total with reduce. Then map each value to Math.round(v / total * 100), or 0 when the total is 0.

stages.hook: Music players, voice recorders, tuners and beat makers are all apps too. Browsers have a full sound studio built in, called the Web Audio API, and you can drive it with JavaScript.
stages.l:
Sound is air wobbling back and forth. Three numbers describe a simple sound:

WordWhat it isYou hear it as
Frequency (Hz)How many wobbles per secondPitch: more wobbles = higher note. The note A is 440 Hz.
Amplitude (gain)How big the wobbles areVolume: 0 is silent, 1 is full volume
WaveformThe shape of each wobbleTone: sine is soft and pure, square is buzzy like old game consoles, sawtooth is bright and harsh

Audio apps connect nodes like guitar pedals: a source (makes sound) → effects (volume, echo, filters) → the destination (your speakers).
stages.p: A tuner app shows a guitar string is playing at 82 Hz, but it should be at 110 Hz.
stages.q: What does the guitarist need to do?
opts: Make the note higher (tighten the string)
miss: Volume is amplitude. The tuner is measuring frequency.
Volume doesn't change the pitch.
The shape changes the tone, not which note it is.
stages.why: Frequency is pitch. 82 Hz is too few wobbles per second, so the note is too low. Tightening the string makes it wobble faster, raising the frequency toward 110 Hz.
stages.h: Frequency is about pitch. Is 82 lower or higher than 110?

stages.l:
On a piano, every key is a semitone apart, and every 12 semitones (an octave) the frequency doubles. So A above middle C is 440 Hz, the next A up is 880 Hz, and the A below is 220 Hz.

The keys in between are spaced evenly by multiplying. Each semitone multiplies the frequency by 2 ** (1 / 12) (about 1.0595). So a note n semitones away from A 440 is:

// ** means "to the power of": 2 ** 3 is 2 × 2 × 2 = 8
const up7 = 440 * 2 ** (7 / 12);   // 7 semitones up from A
console.log(up7.toFixed(2));
659.26

Negative n works too, for notes below A.
stages.p: Write noteFreq(n) that returns the frequency of the note n semitones from A 440, rounded to 2 decimal places as a number.
stages.h: Use the formula from the example with n instead of 7, then round with Math.round(f * 100) / 100.
stages.st:
function noteFreq(n) {
}

stages.l:
To play a note with the Web Audio API, you make an oscillator (a source that wobbles at a frequency), send it through a gain node (volume) to the speakers, start it, and stop it a moment later.

const audio = new AudioContext();     // the sound studio, made once

function beep() {
  const osc = audio.createOscillator();
  const vol = audio.createGain();
  osc.type = "sine";
  osc.frequency.value = 880;           // Hz
  vol.gain.value = 0.1;                // quiet, please
  osc.connect(vol);
  vol.connect(audio.destination);      // destination = the speakers
  osc.start();
  osc.stop(audio.currentTime + 0.2);   // 0.2 seconds from now
  return osc;
}
Volume

Turn your volume down before you test this! Browsers also only allow sound after you've clicked something on the page, so sounds belong in click handlers.
stages.p: Finish playNote(freq): play a "triangle" wave at freq Hz with gain 0.2 for 0.3 seconds, and return the oscillator. Then make clicking a key in #keys play noteFreq of that key's data-n, and show the key's letter and frequency in #now, like A · 440 Hz.
stages.h: Copy the shape of beep, but use freq, "triangle", 0.2 and 0.3. For the keys, one click listener on #keys with e.target.closest("button"), then noteFreq(Number(btn.dataset.n)).

stages.l:
Timers, stopwatches and recorders need code that runs again and again. setInterval(fn, ms) calls fn every ms milliseconds and gives back an id. clearInterval(id) stops it.

let left = 10;
const id = setInterval(() => {
  left--;
  label.textContent = left;
  if (left === 0) clearInterval(id);   // countdown finished
}, 1000);

Keep the id in a variable, set it back to null when stopped, and check it before starting, so pressing Start twice doesn't run two timers at once.
stages.p: Make the stopwatch work. Start adds 1 to tenths every 100 ms and shows the time in #time with one decimal (2.5). Stop pauses it. Reset stops it and shows 0.0. Pressing Start twice must not make it run double speed.
stages.h: Write a show() that sets #time to (tenths / 10).toFixed(1). Start: if timer is null, timer = setInterval(...). Stop: clearInterval(timer); timer = null;. Reset: stop, set tenths = 0, show().

Time to build a whole app: a pocket money tracker. It uses everything from this module: an array of records, a form that creates, a delete button, a total in money format, an empty state and a little bar chart. The page and the render pieces are there. You write the data side.

Make it yours

When you pass, try it in the : add saving with localStorage, a pie chart, or a monthly budget warning.
stages.p:
Write the app:

  1. Add: when #add is submitted, read #what (trimmed), #amount (as a number) and #cat. If the text is empty or the amount isn't more than 0, put Add a name and an amount above 0. in #err and add nothing. Otherwise clear #err, push { id, what, amount, cat } with a new id, clear both boxes and render.
  2. Delete: clicking a .del button removes that item and renders.
  3. render() must also: put the total in #total as US dollars (like $12.50), hide #empty when there are items, and fill #bars with one .row per category that has spending, using barRow(cat, amount, max), where max is the biggest category total.
stages.h: Reuse your own work: money (Intl.NumberFormat), byCategory (group totals), the form pattern from Add with a form, and delegation from Delete with Undo. For the bars: const totals = byCategory(items);, const max = Math.max(...Object.values(totals));, then Object.keys(totals).map(c => barRow(c, totals[c], max)).join("").
